q-336463.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14160679/assets/ea1eb590e18a85672f176188f1bab96d85eb1be92d43edd322d1d032500a97ac.png)

Consider the RL circuit shown above. Given that the current $I(t)$ at time $t$ seconds is given by

$$
I(t)=A{e}^{-14t}+\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),
$$

where $A,$ $\alpha ,$ and $\beta $ are constants, find the value of $\alpha +\beta .$
q-336463.worked_solution:
The diagram shows a series RL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $7\,Ω,$ and an inductor of inductance $\frac{1}{2}\,\text{H}.$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RL circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=7\,Ω.$

$$
{V}_{R}=7I
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=\frac{1}{2}\,\text{H}.$

$$
{V}_{L}=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{dI}{dt}
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of current $I$ in the circuit is

$$
3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)=7I+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{dI}{dt}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}+14I=6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${I}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{I}_{c}}{dt}+14{I}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-14t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $2t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $2t,$ i.e.,

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t), \\ \frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt} & =-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))+14(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) & =6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ 2(-\alpha +7\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2(7\alpha +\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ (-\alpha +7\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+(7\alpha +\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-\alpha +7\beta =3\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\ 7\alpha +\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{3}{50},$ $\beta =\frac{21}{50}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{3}{50}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{21}{50}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)={I}_{c}(t)+{I}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-14t}-\frac{3}{50}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{21}{50}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\alpha =-\frac{3}{50},\,\beta =\frac{21}{50}
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha +\beta  & =-\frac{3}{50}+\frac{21}{50} \\  & =\frac{18}{50} \\  & =\frac{9}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The diagram shows a series RL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of 3sin⁡(2t)V, a resistor of resistance 7Ω, and an inductor of inductance 12H.

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RL circuit, there are two voltage drops:

  • The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality R=7Ω. VR=7I

  • The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality L=12H. VL=12⋅dIdt

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of current I in the circuit is

3sin⁡(2t)=7I+12⋅dIdt

which gives the equation dIdt+14I=6sin⁡(2t).

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

  • To find the complementary solution Ic, we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by dIcdt+14Ic=0. Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution Ic(t)=Ae−14t, where A is a constant of integration.

  • Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument 2t. So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument 2t, i.e., Ip(t)=αcos⁡(2t)+βsin⁡(2t). To find the values of α and β, we substitute Ip=αcos⁡(2t)+βsin⁡(2t),dIpdt=−2αsin⁡(2t)+2βcos⁡(2t), into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side: (−2αsin⁡(2t)+2βcos⁡(2t))+14(αcos⁡(2t)+βsin⁡(2t))=6sin⁡(2t)2(−α+7β)sin⁡(2t)+2(7α+β)cos⁡(2t)=6sin⁡(2t)(−α+7β)sin⁡(2t)+(7α+β)cos⁡(2t)=3sin⁡(2t) Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations: {−α+7β=3(equating the coefficients ofsin⁡(2t))7α+β=0(equating the coefficients ofcos⁡(2t)) Solving this system gives α=−350, β=2150. Therefore, the particular solution is Ip(t)=−350cos⁡(2t)+2150sin⁡(2t).

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

I(t)=Ic(t)+Ip(t)=Ae−14t−350cos⁡(2t)+2150sin⁡(2t).

Therefore, we have α=−350,β=2150 which gives

α+β=−350+2150=1850=925.

q-336643.name: Question 2
q-336643.problem:
The current $I(t),$ in amperes, in a series RL circuit is governed by the differential equation

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}+6I=3,\,I(0)=1.
$$

Find the steady-state current for this circuit.

The steady-state current is
{{field-1}} amperes.
q-336643.worked_solution:
The equation is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${I}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{I}_{c}}{dt}+6{I}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-6t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $0.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $0,$ i.e.,

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\alpha .
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute ${I}_{p}=\alpha $ and $\frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt}=(\alpha )^{′}=0,$ into the inhomogeneous equation:

$$
0+6\alpha =3\,⟹\,\alpha =\frac{1}{2}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is ${I}_{p}(t)=\frac{1}{2}.$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)={I}_{c}(t)+{I}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-6t}+\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${I}_{c}=A{e}^{-6t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The constant ${I}_{p}=\frac{1}{2}$ is the *steady-state current*. As $t\to \infty ,$ the current $I$ approaches the value of the steady-state current.

Therefore, the steady-state current is $\frac{1}{2}$ amperes.

q-336652.name: Question 3
q-336652.problem:
A series RL circuit has a source electromotive force (EMF) of $6\,\text{V},$ a resistance of $30\,Ω,$ and an inductance of $3\,\text{H}.$ Find, **rounded to two decimal places**, the circuit's current after $0.02$ seconds given that the initial current is $1\,\text{A}.$

The current after $0.02$ seconds is
{{field-1}} amperes.
q-336652.worked_solution:
Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RL circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=30\,Ω.$

$$
{V}_{R}=30I
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=3\,\text{H}.$

$$
{V}_{L}=3\,\frac{dI}{dt}
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of current $I$ in the circuit is

$$
6=30I+3\,\frac{dI}{dt}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}+10I=2.
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${I}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{I}_{c}}{dt}+10{I}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-10t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $0.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $0,$ i.e.,

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\alpha .
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute ${I}_{p}=\alpha $ and $\frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt}=(\alpha )^{′}=0,$ into the inhomogeneous equation:

$$
0+10\alpha =2\,⟹\,\alpha =\frac{1}{5}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is ${I}_{p}(t)=\frac{1}{5}.$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)={I}_{c}(t)+{I}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-10t}+\frac{1}{5}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial current of $1\,\text{A}.$ So, we can apply the initial condition $I(0)=1,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}I(0) & =1 \\ A{e}^{-10(0)}+\frac{1}{5} & =1 \\ A & =\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $I(t):$

$$
I(t)=\frac{4}{5}{e}^{-10t}+\frac{1}{5}=\frac{1}{5}(4{e}^{-10t}+1)
$$

Finally, the current in the circuit after $t=0.02$ seconds is

$$
I(0.02)=\frac{1}{5}(4{e}^{-10(0.02)}+1)≈0.85\,\text{A},
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

q-336655.name: Question 4
q-336655.problem:
A series RL circuit has a source electromotive force (EMF) of $8\,\text{V},$ a resistance of $20\,Ω,$ and an inductance of $4\,\text{H}.$
Find, rounded to two decimal places, the circuit's current after $0.02$ seconds given that the initial current is $2\,\text{A}.$

The current after $0.02$ seconds is
{{field-1}} amperes.
q-336655.worked_solution:
Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RL circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=20\,Ω.$

$$
{V}_{R}=20I
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=4\,\text{H}.$

$$
{V}_{L}=4\,\frac{dI}{dt}
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of current $I$ in the circuit is

$$
8=20I+4\,\frac{dI}{dt}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}+5I=2.
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${I}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{I}_{c}}{dt}+5{I}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-5t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $0.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $0,$ i.e.,

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\alpha .
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute ${I}_{p}=\alpha $ and $\frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt}=(\alpha )^{′}=0,$ into the inhomogeneous equation:

$$
0+5\alpha =2\,⟹\,\alpha =\frac{2}{5}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is ${I}_{p}(t)=\frac{2}{5}.$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)={I}_{c}(t)+{I}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-5t}+\frac{2}{5}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial current of $2\,\text{A}.$ So, we can apply the initial condition $I(0)=2,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}I(0) & =2 \\ A{e}^{-5(0)}+\frac{2}{5} & =2 \\ A & =\frac{8}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $I(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & =\frac{8}{5}{e}^{-5t}+\frac{2}{5} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}(4{e}^{-5t}+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the current in the circuit after $t=0.02$ seconds is

$$
I(0.02)=\frac{2}{5}(4{e}^{-5(0.02)}+1)≈1.85\,\text{A},
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

  • The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality R=20Ω. VR=20I

  • The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality L=4H. VL=4dIdt

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of current I in the circuit is 8=20I+4dIdt which gives the equation dIdt+5I=2.

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

  • To find the complementary solution Ic, we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by dIcdt+5Ic=0. Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution Ic(t)=Ae−5t, where A is a constant of integration.

  • Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree 0. So, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree 0, i.e., Ip(t)=α. To find the value of α, we substitute Ip=α and dIpdt=(α)′=0, into the inhomogeneous equation: 0+5α=2⟹α=25 Therefore, the particular solution is Ip(t)=25.

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is I(t)=Ic(t)+Ip(t)=Ae−5t+25.

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial current of 2A. So, we can apply the initial condition I(0)=2, and solve for A: I(0)=2Ae−5(0)+25=2A=85

Therefore, we have the following expression for I(t): I(t)=85e−5t+25=25(4e−5t+1)

Finally, the current in the circuit after t=0.02 seconds is I(0.02)=25(4e−5(0.02)+1)≈1.85A, rounded to two decimal places.

q-336741.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14160679/assets/00d6676b631bd49c0c9b8a82f8dd05de3be6842f18b0c1c6b70f208e1d290d5a.png)

Consider the RL circuit shown above. Given that the current $I(t)$ at time $t$ seconds is given by

$$
I(t)=A{e}^{-12t}+\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t),
$$

where $A,$ $\alpha ,$ and $\beta $ are constants, find the value of $\alpha +\beta .$
q-336741.worked_solution:
The diagram shows a series RL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $3\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $6\,Ω,$ and an inductor of inductance $\frac{1}{2}\,\text{H}.$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RL circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=6\,Ω.$

$$
{V}_{R}=6I
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=\frac{1}{2}\,\text{H}.$

$$
{V}_{L}=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{dI}{dt}
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of current $I$ in the circuit is

$$
3\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)=6I+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{dI}{dt}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}+12I=6\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t).
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${I}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{I}_{c}}{dt}+12{I}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-12t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $5t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $5t,$ i.e.,

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t), \\ \frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt} & =-5\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)+5\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-5\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)+5\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t))+12(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)) & =6\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ (-5\alpha +12\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)+(12\alpha +5\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) & =6\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-5\alpha +12\beta =6\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)) \\ 12\alpha +5\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t))\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{30}{169},$ $\beta =\frac{72}{169}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{30}{169}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\frac{72}{169}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)={I}_{c}(t)+{I}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-12t}-\frac{30}{169}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\frac{72}{169}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\alpha =-\frac{30}{169},\,\beta =\frac{72}{169}
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha +\beta  & =-\frac{30}{169}+\frac{72}{169} \\  & =\frac{42}{169}.\end{aligned}
$$
